definition: Consign means to hand something over into another's care.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word consign. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know consign should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Rather than run the spring sale herself, the sculptor consigned her early bronzes to an auction house in the city.
Lend is the lightest handover, far milder than consign — you stay the owner, expect the thing back shortly, and sign nothing, while consigning puts the transfer of custody on paper.

Deposit is still milder than consign: you place a thing with an institution for safekeeping and can take it back at will, while consigning hands over real custody — recorded, receipted, and often for good.

To entrust is to hand something into another's care while spotlighting your confidence in that person — trust is the whole point. Consign is cooler and transactional: custody changes hands formally, often with paperwork, and says nothing about affection. You entrust a child to a friend; you consign goods to a broker.

Transfer is the flat, neutral word for moving something from one holder to another — money, titles, employees. Consign is narrower and more formal: a recorded handover of custody, the register of auction houses and archives. Every consignment is a transfer, but not every transfer is a consignment.

When the touring company folded, its wardrobe crates were consigned to the drama school across the street — the school stores and mends the costumes, and the receivers may take them back if the company ever re-forms.
Consign is more precise than give or send because it marks a formal transfer of custody: the crates changed keepers, on the record, without necessarily changing owners at all.
Consign is formal and transactional — the register of auction houses, brokers, and archives.
It stresses the handover of custody, often with paperwork, and says nothing about affection; entrust is the warmer choice when your confidence in the keeper is the point.
Consign also has a darker idiom — to consign something to the flames, or to oblivion — meaning to hand it over to a fate.

The vintage jacket had hung in Mara's closet for two years, too good to donate and too big to wear.
The shop on Fifth Street offered a third route: she could consign it, leaving the jacket in the store's care while it looked for a buyer.
The owner wrote a receipt on the spot -- item, condition, asking price, and a sixty-forty division of whatever it fetched.
'You still own it until it sells,' the owner said, sliding the carbon copy across the counter.
'The paper is what makes it official.' Three weeks later a text arrived: sold.
Mara had never met the buyer; the shop's ledger had done all the work for her.
